read_scope.notes: Read all 22 pages, including references and Appendices A–G, from the frozen PDF. Visually inspected every rendered PDF page, all five figures and all twelve tables. Consulted frozen paper.tex and the section locations in specificity_results.tex to resolve wording, links and notation. The abstract contains 152 whitespace-delimited words after normalizing TeX accents and punctuation. Technical appendices were treated as optional depth when assessing main-text accessibility. Extraction and rendering used an isolated temporary directory. No other reviews, previous manuscripts or evaluation records were inspected.

score_reasons.expression: Excellent precision and fluent English. Sections 4.1–4.2 distinguish alignment, error and the no-contrast benchmark with ordinary language before notation; Sections 5.3–5.5 consistently distinguish estimates, resolved comparisons and retrospective checks. Most sentences carry one useful idea, and qualifications have identifiable purposes. The abstract sentence about uncertainty preventing an established improvement is a localized opportunity for more direct wording.
score_reasons.structure: The main text progresses coherently from a concrete evaluation problem through the reference panel, controlled clauses, measurements, score intuition and primary results to explanatory diagnostics. Section 4.4 announces the retrospective work, and derivations, older interventions and provenance remain in optional appendices. Section 5.4 could distinguish its two successive changes of evaluation more visibly: averaging scenes and rescaling contrasts have different meanings despite sharing a table and an ordering-change heading.
score_reasons.new_reader_understanding: The intended reader can recover the complete study without the repository or appendices. The six conditions, fixed scene design, equal painter weighting, development-IQR units and finite digital target are explicit. The lightness example and the 1/0/1 idealized error examples are particularly effective. Figures 1–3 and Tables 2–5 supply interpretable comparisons, including uncertainty and benchmark meanings. Remaining friction is local to the compressed abstract inference sentence and the transition between aggregation and calibration in Section 5.4.
score_reasons.engagement: The opening Monet–Sisley example establishes a consequential question, Figure 1 supplies an inspectable visual case, and the findings develop through useful reversals: alignment without low error, an uneven painter response, and different lowest estimates after aggregation or calibration. Figures are legible and their captions tell the reader what to compare. The discussion becomes general reporting advice just before a substantial limitations paragraph; grounding that advice in the concrete FLUX/GPT Image 2 comparison would give the narrative a more satisfying payoff.

strengths: Section 4.1, page 5, uses a measured Monet–Sisley lightness gap and three idealized generators to explain centering and the different meanings of aligned response and total error before introducing equations.

Sections 4.2–4.3, pages 5–6, clearly explain repeat correction, its independence assumptions, the theoretical D = 1 benchmark, and the limited interpretation of intervals across fourteen fixed briefs.

Figure 1, page 4, makes all six clauses and model configurations visually comparable, identifies the unmatched reference examples, and gives a deterministic selection rule rather than implying representative perceptual validation.
Figures 2–3, pages 7–8, connect aggregate geometry to labeled painter pairs. Magnified Monet/Sisley/Pissarro views, numeric heatmaps and explicit benchmark captions reward inspection.
Section 5.5 and Table 5, pages 9–10, report exactly which model comparisons change after source correction and identify the newly resolved GPT Image 1 comparison as retrospective.
The main text remains independently understandable while Appendices A–G preserve technical details, supporting cohorts, the contrary transfer result and source/model-provenance limitations.

findings.issue: The central inference is expressed through the nested construction “uncertainty prevents establishing lower mismatch than a predictor making no painter distinctions.” The meaning is correct, but this is the abstract’s least direct sentence.
findings.reader_effect: A new reader must unpack a statement about uncertainty and a counterfactual predictor while also distinguishing partial alignment from error.
findings.suggested_change: Replace the sentence with: “Before calibration, every model partly aligns with the reference differences, but none is shown to have lower mismatch than making no painter distinctions.” This preserves the bounded conclusion and reduces the word count within the 155-word limit.

findings.location: Section 5.4 and Table 4, page 9; specificity_results.tex lines 86–108
findings.issue: The subsection presents two ordering changes in quick succession: Nano Banana 2 versus FLUX after scene averaging, then GPT Image 2 versus FLUX after calibration. The explanations are present, but the transition between the two operations is visually understated.
findings.reader_effect: A scanning reader can initially treat these as variants of one adjustment, although one changes aggregation and the other fits a multiplier to the contrasts.
findings.suggested_change: Use short paragraph lead-ins such as “Averaging scenes” and “Rescaling contrasts,” replacing words in the existing paragraph openings. Keep Table 4 and all estimates; the goal is a clearer transition without adding a section or page.

findings.location: Section 6, opening paragraph, page 10; paper.tex lines 312–317
findings.issue: The discussion opens with general advice about recommendations rather than explicitly connecting that advice to the paper’s concrete model trade-off.
findings.reader_effect: The final interpretation is less memorable than the preceding results, despite the strong evidence for why the choice of evaluation matters.
findings.suggested_change: Replace the opening general sentence with a concrete synthesis, for example: “FLUX’s lowest uncalibrated error and GPT Image 2’s lowest calibrated error answer different evaluation questions; neither aggregate result alone resolves Monet–Sisley matching.” Retain the existing requirements to report the target, features and uncertainty, trimming the paragraph to its present length.

summary: An excellent and self-contained account of a bounded digital-reference comparison. The main narrative explains the design and score meanings, separates primary inference from retrospective diagnostics, and avoids converting measured agreement into perceptual fidelity. Only localized wording, navigation and closing-synthesis refinements remain; no additional evidence or length is needed.
